paras: The threatened lynching of Henry McNeal took place in Lawton, Oklahoma, on 21 August 1915, when a mob began forming to take McNeal, a 30-year-old Black man accused of attempting to assault a white woman. He was moved from the city jail to the guard house at Fort Sill, and no one was killed. An Oklahoma paper described the episode as a narrowly averted "race war," and the Indianapolis Freeman reported that Black residents, many of them women dressed as men, had driven the mob off.

According to a dispatch from Fort Sill, Mrs. Frank Leonard, the wife of a patent medicine salesman, said that a man entered her Lawton home at about 8 o'clock on Saturday night, locked the door behind him, and went upstairs. In her account, she was tending her babies in a darkened room when he put his hand over her mouth, and when she ran screaming to the door he climbed out of a window and fled. McNeal was arrested about two hours later and taken to the city jail.

As "a determined mob began forming," McNeal was "quietly and quickly" taken to Fort Sill. The Guthrie Daily Leader reported that he was "placed in charge of the soldiers" there. On 24 August he was held in the guard house under strong guard, "awaiting developments" at Lawton.
No report of charges, a trial, or McNeal's release was found in the coverage, and none of the reports names any member of the mob.

The Guthrie Daily Leader carried the first report on 23 August under the headline "Race War Averted at Lawton," stating as fact that there had been "an attempted assault by a negro on a white woman." The Oklahoma City Times printed the fullest account the next day, naming McNeal and Mrs. Leonard and attributing the charge with "it is alleged" and "according to the woman's story." A Kansas weekly, the Liberal Democrat, reprinted the dispatch's opening paragraph in its Oklahoma news column on 3 September, without "it is alleged."

The only Black-press notice found was an editorial paragraph in the Indianapolis Freeman of 4 September, which cited "a report from Lawton" without naming McNeal. The Freeman suggested that "the women are to play an important part in setting at naught the mob" and placed the virtue "on the side of those who stand up against the assailants of their liberties." Where the white reports treated the episode as a crime story with a prisoner quietly saved, the Freeman presented it as an act of Black self-defense.

The accounts differ on why the mob did not act. The Oklahoma reports credit the prisoner's quick removal to Fort Sill and say nothing of resistance, although the Guthrie paper called the episode a narrowly averted "race war." The Freeman's version, that the mob "was beaten off by Negroes, many of whom were women who dressed themselves as men," is secondhand and does not appear in the white reports found.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Henry McNeal
bases: A mob formed at Lawton to seize and, per the Black press, hang a Black prisoner accused of attempted assault, and officials removed him to Fort Sill; no one was killed (A1, A2, A5).

A mob formed to take McNeal, who was accused of attempted assault on a white woman, but he was moved to Fort Sill and no killing is reported (A1, A2, A5); this is a threatened lynching, not a completed one.
Two differently worded Oklahoma reports (A1, A2) and a Black-press report from Lawton (A5) agree that a mob formed and the prisoner was taken to Fort Sill, though A5 differs on why the mob failed.

accounts.label: Oklahoma press reports (Guthrie, Fort Sill dispatch)
accounts.gist: A mob began forming after the arrest, and the prisoner was quietly hastened from the Lawton city jail to Fort Sill before it could act.

accounts.label: The accuser's story
accounts.gist: A man entered the Leonard home, locked the door, went upstairs, and put his hand over her mouth in a darkened room; she ran screaming and he fled through a window.

accounts.label: Report from Lawton cited by the Indianapolis Freeman
accounts.gist: The mob that formed to hang the prisoner was beaten off by Black residents, many of them women dressed as men, and the prisoner was rushed to Fort Sill.

framing.detail: The Guthrie Daily Leader headed its brief 'Race War Averted at Lawton' and stated the assault as fact: 'an attempted assault by a negro on a white woman.'
The Oklahoma City Times attributed the charge ('it is alleged', 'according to the woman's story') and called the prisoner 'the negro' throughout.
The Liberal Democrat's state-news column reprinted the dispatch's first paragraph without 'it is alleged'.
The Freeman held up the Lawton women as a model for 'setting at naught the mob' and placed 'the virtue' with those who resist.

versions.value: Officials quietly and quickly moved the prisoner to Fort Sill while the mob was forming
Black residents, many of them women dressed as men, beat off the mob, and the prisoner was rushed to Fort Sill

conflicts.note: The Oklahoma reports are closer to the event and more detailed but say nothing of Black resistance; the Guthrie paper's phrase 'race war' fits a confrontation but does not describe one. The Freeman's version is secondhand ('a report from Lawton') and not found in any white paper.
